title: Sum of Powers: Extension to Non-Integer Exponents
description: Extends Faulhaber's formulas to real exponents via the p-series ζ(s) = ∑ 1/n^s. Proves convergence dichotomy (iff s > 1), recovers ζ(2) = π²/6 and ζ(4) = π⁴/90, establishes term and zeta monotonicity, and bridges real-exponent theory to integer power sums.

overview.historicalContext: Johann Faulhaber (1631) published closed-form expressions for sums of consecutive kth powers, extending work by al-Haytham (c. 1000) and Bernoulli. The reciprocal series sum 1/n^2 was posed as the Basel Problem by Pietro Mengoli in 1644 and resisted solution for 90 years. Euler's breakthrough in 1734, showing zeta(2) = pi^2/6, stunned contemporary mathematicians by linking a discrete arithmetic sum to the circle constant. Euler subsequently computed zeta(2k) for all positive integers k using Bernoulli numbers and powers of pi. The convergence dichotomy at s = 1 — the harmonic series diverges while sum 1/n^s converges for any s > 1 — was first observed by Nicole Oresme (c. 1360) and later connected to the prime number theorem via the Euler product zeta(s) = prod (1 - p^{-s})^{-1}. Riemann's 1859 memoir extended zeta(s) to complex s via analytic continuation, transforming number theory forever.
overview.problemStatement: Extend Faulhaber integer power sums to real exponents via zeta(s) = sum 1/n^s.
overview.text: A 175-line formalization extending Faulhaber's integer power sum formulas to real exponents via the Riemann zeta function $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$. The proof establishes the convergence dichotomy (the $p$-series converges iff $s > 1$), recovers the Basel problem $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$ and $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/90$ from Mathlib, proves term-wise and sum-wise antitonicity of $\zeta(s)$ in $s$, derives bounds $1 \leq \zeta(s) \leq \pi^2/6$ for $s \geq 2$, shows partial sum convergence and monotonicity, and bridges real-exponent theory back to integer power sums via `rpow_natCast`. All 14 theorems are fully verified with 0 sorries and 0 axioms, building on Mathlib's `summable_nat_rpow_inv`, `hasSum_zeta_two`, and `hasSum_zeta_four`.
overview.proofStrategy: Eight parts: convergence dichotomy, known values, term monotonicity, zeta monotonicity, bounds, partial sums, bridge to integers. Fully verified.

conclusion.summary: All 14 results fully proved. 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications:
**1. Convergence dichotomy**: The sharp threshold $s > 1$ for convergence of $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 1/n^s$ is fundamental to analysis. The divergence at $s = 1$ (harmonic series) connects to the infinitude of primes via Euler's product formula $\zeta(s) = \prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1}$.

**2. Bridge to number theory**: This formalization bridges Faulhaber's combinatorial integer power sums $\sum_{k=1}^n k^m$ to the analytic zeta function $\zeta(s) = \sum 1/n^s$. The zeta function is the Rosetta stone of number theory: its zeros encode the distribution of primes (Riemann hypothesis), its special values encode deep arithmetic invariants (class numbers, regulators), and its Euler product connects additive and multiplicative number theory.

**3. Special values and Bernoulli numbers**: The verified values $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$ (Basel problem) and $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/90$ are instances of Euler's general formula $\zeta(2k) = (-1)^{k+1} B_{2k} (2\pi)^{2k} / (2(2k)!)$ where $B_{2k}$ are Bernoulli numbers. The odd zeta values $\zeta(3), \zeta(5), \ldots$ remain mysterious — Apéry (1979) proved $\zeta(3)$ irrational, but the irrationality of $\zeta(5)$ is open.

**4. Monotonicity and functional analysis**: The proved monotonicity $s_1 < s_2 \Rightarrow \zeta(s_1) > \zeta(s_2)$ for $s > 1$ reflects the strict decrease of the zeta function on the real line, with $\zeta(s) \to \infty$ as $s \to 1^+$ and $\zeta(s) \to 1$ as $s \to \infty$.
openQuestions: Can $\zeta(2k)$ for $k = 3, 4, \ldots$ be computed from Bernoulli numbers in Lean? The formula $\zeta(2k) = (-1)^{k+1} B_{2k} (2\pi)^{2k} / (2(2k)!)$ would give $\zeta(6) = \pi^6/945$, $\zeta(8) = \pi^8/9450$, etc.

Can the Euler product formula $\zeta(s) = \prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ be formalized? This would connect the additive definition (sum over naturals) to the multiplicative structure (product over primes), providing a new proof of the infinitude of primes

Can the functional equation $\zeta(s) = 2^s \pi^{s-1} \sin(\pi s/2) \Gamma(1-s) \zeta(1-s)$ be stated and the analytic continuation to $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{1\}$ formalized? This is the key ingredient connecting the Riemann hypothesis to prime distribution

crossReferences.description: Extends integer power sums to real exponents
Uses zeta(2) = pi^2/6 for upper bounds

The Riemann hypothesis concerns the zeros of the analytic continuation of $\zeta(s)$ to $\mathbb{C}$. This entry formalizes the real-valued restriction $\zeta(s)$ for $s > 1$, providing the starting point for the full complex theory

The divergence of $\sum 1/p$ (Euler, 1737) follows from the Euler product $\zeta(s) = \prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ and the divergence of $\zeta(s)$ as $s \to 1^+$. Both results concern the growth rate of the harmonic-type series that this entry's convergence dichotomy classifies

Stirling's formula $n! \sim \sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n$ involves the same $\pi$ that appears in $\zeta(2k) = (-1)^{k+1} B_{2k} (2\pi)^{2k} / (2(2k)!)$. Both arise from the Gamma function $\Gamma(s)$, which appears in the functional equation of $\zeta(s)$

Euler's proof of the infinitude of primes (1737) uses $\zeta(s) \to \infty$ as $s \to 1^+$ combined with the Euler product: if primes were finite, $\prod_p (1-p^{-1})^{-1}$ would be a finite product, contradicting the divergence
